entries.title: Nationals 3, Tigers 1: Game Recap
entries.summary: Washington took a 1-0 lead in the second on a long homer to right-center field by CJ Abrams.
entries.content:
By Dave Hogg

CJ Abrams hit a tiebreaking two-run homer and added a solo shot to give the Washington Nationals a 3-1 victory over the Detroit Tigers on Tuesday night.

The Nationals won for the seventh time in 10 games, while Detroit dropped to 2-5 in its last seven. The Tigers have scored exactly one run in all five losses, while scoring nine and 11 runs in the two wins.

Both teams are 74-84 with four games left in the season.

Jackson Kent (2-4) picked up the win in relief of Nationals opener Riley Cornelio. Kent pitched four innings, allowing one unearned run on six hits and two walks. Erik Tolman pitched the ninth for his fourth save.

Tigers starter Drew Anderson (5-7) took the loss, allowing three runs on five hits. He struck out five without walking a batter.

Washington took a 1-0 lead in the second on a long homer to right-center field by Abrams. That gave him 100 RBIs to go along with his 30 homer/30 stolen base season.

The Tigers tied the game in the sixth when Ben Malgeri scored on Kent's second wild pitch of the inning. Washington also missed two opportunities to turn double plays in the inning.

Abrams then hit a two-run homer in the seventh, his 33rd of the season, to end Anderson's night.

Up nextThe teams finish their three-game series on Wednesday afternoon with Tigers LHP Framber Valdez (10-11, 4.06) facing a yet-to-be-announced Nationals starter.

entries.title: Mystics 79, Sun 69: Game Recap
entries.summary: The Mystics stretched their lead over Dallas and New York (tied for seventh) to one game with two days remaining in the regular season.
entries.content:
Shakira Austin had 25 points and 13 rebounds to help the Washington Mystics beat the Connecticut Sun 79-69 on Tuesday night for their franchise-record 27th win of the season.

Washington (27-16) set the previous mark of 26 wins in 2019, en route to the franchise’s only WNBA championship.

The Mystics stretched their lead over Dallas and New York (tied for seventh) to one game with two days remaining in the regular season.

Diamond Miller led Connecticut (10-33) with 19 points. Leila Lacan and Raegan Beers scored 11 points apiece.

Washington used a 15-4 run to push its lead into double figures with 3:26 left in the third quarter and Cotie McMahon hit a 3 about 90 seconds later that made it 66-53.

McMahon had 13 points and Sonia Citron 12 for the Mystics.

Austin made a career-high 11 free throws, extended her single-season franchise record to 397 rebounds and had her 20th double-double this season. Austin and Kiki Iraiafen (22 double-doubles) are the first teammates in WNBA history with at least 20 double-doubles in the same season.

The Sun outrebounded Washington 43-34. The Mystics have outrebounded their opponents a WNBA-record 39 times this season.

entries.title: Flights Are Resuming at DCA After Runway Light Failure
entries.summary: A ground stop triggered delays and cancellations for hours Tuesday night.
entries.content:
A major runway was again open at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport after several flights were delayed or canceled Tuesday night when a lighting equipment failure forced the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a ground stop, according to DCA officials.

At around 10:20 p.m., officials announced that crews had restored the malfunctioning runway lights, but warned travelers to expect residual delays throughout the night.

According to FAA alerts, the lighting system on the airport's busiest and longest runway was not working, forcing authorities to issue significant delays.

The FAA halted all flights departing to DCA through 10:30 p.m., causing airlines to cancel over 43 flights, with departures delayed by about an hour on average, according to FlightAware.

This story has been updated with the reopening of DCA’s longest runway.

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Sept. 25)
entries.summary: Theatre Week begins, “The Firebird” takes flight and a Eurovision star lands at Black Cat.
entries.content:
Thursday

Theatre Week
Various DMV Theaters, $25 to $65, through Oct. 11

Over an 18-day stretch, 27 area theaters have blocked off a set number of seats at discount prices. Admittedly, 18 days is not a “week,” but to (loosely) quote the musical “Rent,” how do you measure a season of love? Should your first choice show at a larger theater sell out, Theatre Week is a great time to try a smaller local company. Free events include today’s pop-up serenades at Dulles and DCA, a concert at The Wharf on Sept. 29 and a “State of DC Theatre” podcast taping at Studio Theatre on Oct. 5.

“Lay Him Quietly” at Dance Place
3225 8th St. NE, 7 p.m. free, registration required

A decade ago, Dance Place hosted touring dance companies multiple times each month. Now, it’s only a few times a year, as the Brookland venue struggles with fiscal issues and leadership turnover. There’s a bright spot this Wednesday and Thursday, however, when the Swedish embassy presents a free immersive work by Hiroki Ichinose, a Japanese-American dance artist and member of Göteborg Operans Danskompani. Ichinose and fellow Swedish dancer Ninos Josef perform “Lay Him Quietly” before a film backdrop, a now-rare chance to see intimate international modern dance in the District.

More to explore: Photographer Sheila Pree Bright talks American flag imagery at the National Gallery of Art

Friday

All Things Go Music Festival 
Merriweather Post Pavilion, Columbia, tickets start at $170

Great news for anyone who has ever wanted to yell, “Summer isn’t over yet!” at the top of their lungs in late September: Swedish superstar and “Midnight Sun” singer Zara Larsson is among the headliners at this year’s All Things Go Music Festival. The 2026 lineup has more female boldfaced names than Lilith Fair. Mitski is the big draw on Friday, Hayley Williams and Larsson on Saturday and Brandi Carlile on Sunday.

Dance Theatre of Harlem at The National Theatre
1321 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, 7:30 (Also 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Saturday), $76 to $114

Washington Performing Arts first presented Dance Theatre of Harlem way back in 1973, four years after Arthur Mitchell founded his groundbreaking company dedicated to Black excellence in ballet. Given that a festival of Black dance was among the events cancelled at the Kennedy Center earlier this year, it’s all the more meaningful that WPA is welcoming Dance Theatre of Harlem back to town. The performance includes George Balanchine’s “Donizetti Variations,” a soulful suite set to music by Aretha Franklin and James Brown.

More to explore: IZIS at the Publick Playhouse

Saturday

MARO at The Black Cat
1811 14th St. NW, 7:30, $30

At every Eurovision Song Context, there’s a balladeer who’s too sincere to win the crystal trophy and confetti, but who wins over the crowd and launches an international career. In 2022 that act was MARO. For an easy-listening initiation, check out her dreamy cover of Harry Styles’ “As it Was” with Charlotte Cardin and November Ultra. Sadly, MARO’s spring North American tour was cancelled due to what the singer called “circumstances beyond our control.” That’s usually code for failure to secure a U.S. visa, all the better reason to turn out now that the Portuguese singer and her band made it to America.

Music From the Sole at George Mason University
4373 Mason Pond Drive, Fairfax, 7:30, $38 to $60, minors half price

Like dance? Got a car, or willing to spend time on public transit? Great, because it’s time to start schlepping to George Mason University if you want to see touring companies of Kennedy Center-caliber. The Center for the Arts’ 2026-27 dance season kicks off with Music From the Sole, a dance-and-music collective with Brazilian and Afro-Cuban influences, plus “flashes of samba, house, Lindy Hop and Orisha dances,” according to The New York Times review of “I Didn’t Come to Stay.” That’s the work they’ll perform here too, infused with a “party spirit” worth the drive to Fairfax.

More to explore: FiestaDC celebrates Latino Heritage Month on Pennsylvania Avenue.

Sunday 

Takoma Park Folk Festival
Takoma Park Middle School, 10:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., free

DMV neighborhood street fair season continues this weekend with a daylong celebration in The People’s Republic of Takoma Park, as some residents call their counter-culture enclave on the D.C.-Maryland border. The festival’s seven stages feature folk musicians, world music and children’s entertainment. There’s also a juried craft show, community tabling and two-dozen food vendors, most offering vegan and gluten-free options.

Black Women Make Movies at Shanklin Hall
2325 18th St. NW, 5 to 8 p.m, $23

Catch five short films at this event billed as a “screening + mixer” for “Black women filmmakers and the folx who love them.” Local documentaries in the lineup explore underground “numbers” gambling in the 1960s and “The Legacy of Lee’s Flower Shop,” one of D.C.’s oldest Black-owned businesses. Bonus: One drink is included with each ticket.

More to explore: Alexandria Symphony performs at the George Washington Masonic Memorial

entries.title: What to Expect From Xi’s Big Visit: Kicked Cans
entries.summary: Trump will roll out the red carpet for the Chinese leader, but current and former officials don’t envision big breakthroughs during the talks.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump will welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington for a state visit as the pair seeks to deepen their personal relationship and maintain some future stability.

The governments — which at times have been adversarial — have made slow progress on the tangible commitments agreed to in May when Trump visited Beijing. But the countries remain locked in strategic competitions bubbling beneath the surface of the leaders’ relationship. And it’s unlikely, according to experts and current and former U.S. officials who spoke with The Washington Sun, that a big breakthrough on the most profound sticking points will come during Xi’s visit.

“I think the status quo with China is not great by any stretch, but it's better than the alternative: a tariff war and a limited supply of our rare critical minerals,” said one U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak candidly. “So I think that the expectation is it's mostly going to be kicking the can.”

When Xi touches down Wednesday evening at Joint Base Andrews, it will kick off a couple of days of intense diplomacy. The world leaders last saw one another in May, when Trump traveled to Beijing for three days of events in which the Chinese regaled him with pomp and red carpets. That olive branch is expected to be reciprocated by the United States, which is preparing to pull out all the stops.

“The optics and the pageantry are really the point of this trip” — to show the strength of Xi and Trump’s relationship, Sara Schuman, a former senior U.S. negotiator for China trade and managing director at Beacon Global Strategies, told The Sun. The optics, she said, will likely “exceed the commercial deliverables.”

“The relationship is the circuit breaker that’s needed to manage the tensions beneath the surface, so they don’t break through,” Schuman said.

It’s expected to be an eventful summit — crammed with tours, military displays and meals — to fulfill Trump’s long-held desire to bring Xi back to Washington. Though Xi was in the United States in 2023, the Chinese leader’s last state visit was in 2015, during the Obama administration. It occurred coincidentally on the same dates — Sept. 24 and 25 — that he’ll visit with Trump.

Following Wednesday’s arrival ceremony, Trump and first lady Melania Trump will host Xi and his wife, Madam Peng Liyuan, at the White House on Thursday. They’ll hold a ceremony on the South Lawn and state floor, marked by 479 military personnel representing all branches of the U.S. military, according to the Office of the First Lady.

The Marine Band will play the Chinese and U.S. national anthems, and a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber and four F-22 Raptors will highlight a military display in a Rose Garden ceremony before a bilateral meeting takes place.

Trump and Xi are scheduled to address the crowd at Thursday evening’s state dinner. Prominent technology industry leaders are expected to attend, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and SpaceX and Tesla founder Elon Musk, according to a senior U.S. official.

NVIDIA AI Jensen Huang AP - 25301665725231 (4126x2751, AR: 1.50)
“The Chinese are reluctant to have top officials come to Washington for anything other than a state visit, and it has to be treated like it. It has something to do with their sense of protocol and standing. And so a state dinner is an essential component of a state visit, along with all the bells and whistles,” said Daniel R. Russel, who served as the assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during Xi’s 2015 state visit.

The summit will wrap up on Friday with a tour of the National Archives and America’s founding documents, after the Trumps host Xi and his wife for tea at the White House.

Not everyone favors the expected display of extravagance, including some of Trump's allies. Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) said in a floor speech on Tuesday that he “would have suggested the president not invite [Xi] to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States” if Trump had asked the senator, calling Xi a “brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator.”

The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

During Trump’s May trip to China, the leaders agreed to a one-year truce of sorts, called “strategic stability.” It aimed to prevent an escalation of tensions or a deliberate chokehold on critical commodities like U.S. export controls or China’s rare earth minerals. And that truce came with three broad agreements on issues central to the White House's goals.

U.S. officials said the two countries agreed to set up both a board of trade and a board of investments. The officials also said China would address Washington’s concerns over the supply chain for critical and rare earth minerals in addition to agreeing to purchase $17 billion worth of American agricultural products, prorated for 2026, in addition to commitments China had previously made to buy soybeans — a deal the Chinese said was never confirmed. And Trump said China had agreed to make an initial purchase of 200 American-made Boeing aircraft.

Of the three, the agreement to create a board of trade has seen the most significant movement, experts tracking the progress say. When first announced, the White House said in a document the board of trade would allow both countries “to manage bilateral trade across non-sensitive goods.” The U.S. set up a public comment period for the proposed board, a necessary step toward formally establishing it. And American officials seem poised to roll it out, coupled with some tariff relief.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested as much in a Monday interview, telling CNBC that both sides discussed lowering tariffs on “noncritical” items.

But there has been no public movement on the board of investment, which the White House said was intended to provide a forum to discuss “investment-related issues.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week during an interview with Fox News that China has made progress toward buying the 200 Boeing planes initially agreed upon, but no purchase has been announced. Trump has said the deal eventually was expected to be for 750 planes, though Greer did not mention anything about additional aircraft. The U.S. official said the deal had been on thin ice after disagreements between China and Boeing. The White House initially touted the agreement as a significant victory for the Trump administration because it had been years since China purchased Boeing planes.

Jamieson Greer AP-25099609540207 (7476x4984, AR: 1.50)
“There's a long history of teeing up ideas and possibilities and then sort of at the eleventh hour the Chinese will come in with some condition and crater it essentially,” said Russel. “It’s done for strategic reasons. It's the way they operate to try and keep everything all balanced and so they can, in part, test what the U.S. really wants.”

Concerning the agricultural agreement — the issue perhaps most closely aligned with the president’s domestic agenda — those tracking the purchases say China has made significant progress buying soybeans from American farmers. As of Sept. 11, the American Soybean Association estimates Chinese buyers have ordered 15.5 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans this season. China committed to buy at least 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans this marketing year.

But agricultural purchases outside of soybeans are lacking. Ishan Bhanu, the lead agricultural commodities analyst at the data firm Kpler, says other American products China would likely buy include corn, wheat, cotton and peanuts. Bhanu said those purchases have been slower to materialize, with only $3 billion bought so far — equating to roughly a half-billion per month.

“When we cut the data — call it pro-rated since May or since June — anyway we look at it, there has been no progress towards this commitment,” Bhanu said. Bhanu said corn is the only commodity that China buys in excess that would meet its commitments. But the large amount needed would send corn prices in both the U.S. and abroad skyrocketing, he said, creating an additional problem for the countries.

The fight over critical minerals and the supply chain remains the issue on which the U.S. and China have struggled to bridge their gap. Two sources say the Trump administration believes China has done the bare minimum to live up to the May agreement, which the document circulated by the White House said would also address U.S. concern about China blocking Americans from purchasing rare earth production equipment.

“No surprise,” the U.S. official said, adding that China doesn’t “live up to their commitments, ever.”

Schuman predicted that the lack of progress on addressing the critical mineral issue would factor into whether the U.S. extends the one-year “strategic stability” truce.

Ultimately, Xi’s visit is significant, though it’s expected to produce less-than-significant results. But any progress at all could be enough for the Trump administration to consider it a win, according to multiple people familiar with the relationship.

Ryan Hass, who served on the White House National Security Council from 2013 to 2017, said achieving small diplomatic gains would be a positive development, given the precarious dynamics between the world’s preeminent superpowers.

“I don’t think there will be any great surprises,” said Hass, who is now the director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution. “President Trump is just preternaturally predisposed to highlight and tout the fact that China wants to buy American products.”
entries.author: Jasmine Wright, Ben T.N. Mause
